Q: How to use CMake's ProcessorCount for building? A:

This is how I have done it. Apparently there is no way to configure CMake standalone, but this works with but the usual Linux CLI tools.

1. create a CMakePresets.json to provide (mandatory) configurePresets for your buildPresets:

{
    "version": 3,
    "cmakeMinimumRequired": {
        "major": 3,
        "minor": 22
    },
    "configurePresets": [{
        "name": "default",
        "binaryDir": "build",
        "environment": { "CMAKE_CONFIGURATION_TYPES": "RelWithDebug" },
        "generator": "Ninja Multi-Config"
    }]
}

Everything in this one is just an example - enter whatever fits your project.

2. create a template cmake/CMakeUserPresets.json.template with an easily found placeholder string:

{
    "version": 3,
    "cmakeMinimumRequired": {
        "major": 3,
        "minor": 22
    },
    "buildPresets": [{
        "name": "default",
        "configurePreset": "default",
        "environment": { "CMAKE_DEFAULT_BUILD_TYPE": "RelWithDebInfo" },
        "jobs": !!JOB_COUNT!!
    }]
}

Everything but the "jobs": !!JOB_COUNT!! line in this one is just an example - enter whatever fits your project.

3. create a sed file cmake/cpuinfo.sed that prints the desired process count when fed /proc/cpuinfo:

s/cpu[[:space:]]+cores[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*([[:digit:]]+)/\1/p
T
q

This one grabs the physical CPU count, to ensure I can continue to do arbitrary other tasks on the same machine.
On something like a private build server, or if you use the xkcd method, you may try to use logical count instead, but usually building is disk-bound anyway, so do not expect large gains. The greatest speed-up is going from 1 to 2, and in my experience little differs past 4.

4. create a script file generate-user-presets.bash that replaces the placeholder:

#!/bin/bash
cd "$(dirname "$0")" || exit
cores=$(sed --quiet --regexp-extended --file=cmake/cpuinfo.sed /proc/cpuinfo)
sed --expression="s/!!JOB_COUNT!!/$cores/" cmake/CMakeUserPresets.json.template >CMakeUserPresets.json

Now any user can execute the .bash file to generate presets with the correct process count... preset.

You can additionally use the sentinel pattern to enforce usage of the preset, to safeguard against forgetting to use the preset.

If you use an IDE like CLion, it picks up the presets automatically, so there is no real need to add sentinel code, which is why I omitted it here for brevity.

(Myself, I have come to include it in all my CMake projects just in case - it will create comprehensible error messages e.g. on a CI server, where there is no IDE.)

Q: How does yacc parse C fragments? A:

The POSIX standard specifies a Yacc grammar for Yacc, and that grammar leaves out the details of parsing the action contents:

act   : '{'
        {
          /* Copy action, translate $$, and so on. */
        }
        '}'

There is a sentence in the description which says: An action is an arbitrary C statement and as such can do input or output, call subprograms, and alter external variables. An action is one or more C statements enclosed in curly braces '{' and '}'. The statements shall not contain unbalanced curly brace preprocessing tokens.

The standard seems to neither require nor prohibit doing actual C statement parsing within the actions, but suggests that a minimum parsing is required involving counting balancing parantheses.

Doing a complete parsing job might not be feasible in a Yacc implementation for the following reason. Parsing a fragment of C syntax, in general, requires access to the declarations about all identifiers that are referenced in that syntax, but not defined there. There are grammar ambiguities in C that require information from declarations. This means that the Yacc would have to perform all the header file inclusions as it is parsing the grammar file and implement significant. Implemnetations of Yacc don't require this though; a #include "foo.h" appearing in the file can refer to a header which does not exist at Yacc-processing time; only the translated file (such as y.tab.c) then requires the header to exist when it is processed by a C compiler. Those two processing phases need not take place in the same environment.

A Yacc implementation should probably perform some minimizing tokenizing of the material after the opening curly brace, and count curly braces to determine the closing. It should recognize string and character literals, as well as comments. It should not be fooled by code like "Hello, $1" or case '}': break;. However, say the action does something like { enum foo { $1, $2 }; typedef int $$; }. There, I would say, "all bets are off".

The source code to various Yacc implementations like Berkeley Yacc and Bison is available; it's possible to understand the actual practice.
